claim: The cell surface proteome, termed the surfaceome, serves as the main communication hub between a cell and the extracellular environment.
source: The cell surface proteome, termed the surfaceome, serves as the main communication hub between a cell and the extracellular environment (Wollscheid et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wollscheid et al., 2009

claim: The cell surface compartment often reveals the first signs of cellular distress and disease.
source: As such, this cellular compartment often reveals the first signs of cellular distress and disease, and is of substantial interest to the medical community for diagnostic and therapeutic development (Leth-Larsen et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leth-Larsen et al., 2010

claim: Several strategies have emerged for surfaceomics, including biocytin hydrazide labeling of surface glycoproteins.
source: Several strategies have emerged for either selective or comprehensive surfaceomics, including biocytin hydrazide labeling of surface glycoproteins (Wollscheid et al., 2009), chemical biotinylation of lysines via NHS-ester labeling (Huang, 2012), and promiscuous biotinylator fusion proteins (APEX2, BioID, and SPPLAT) (Rees et al., 2015; Sears et al., 2019; Wollscheid et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wollscheid et al., 2009; Huang, 2012; Rees et al., 2015; Sears et al., 2019

claim: Membrane protein enrichment is necessary due to the inherent low abundance of membrane proteins compared to cytosolic proteins.
source: Membrane protein enrichment is a necessary step in surfaceomics, due to the inherent low abundance of membrane proteins compared to cytosolic proteins, and their identification can be overwhelmed by cytosolic contaminants.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about membrane protein abundance

claim: Current surfaceomics methods require large sample inputs (biocytin hydrazide).
source: While each of these strategies robustly label surface proteins, they: (1) require large sample inputs (biocytin hydrazide), (2) require production of genetically engineered cells (APEX2 and BioID), (3) label only partner proteins by binding targeting antibodies fused to APEX2 or horseradish peroxidase (HRP; SPPLAT), (4) require extensive sample manipulation (biocytin hydrazide), or (5) exhibit increased nonspecific labeling (NHS-ester, Table 1; Bausch-Fluck et al., 2012; Elschenbroich et al., 2010; Griffin and Schnitzer, 2011; Kuhlmann et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple sources including Bausch-Fluck et al., 2012; Elschenbroich et al., 2010; Griffin and Schnitzer, 2011; Kuhlmann et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020b

claim: Current surfaceomics methods require production of genetically engineered cells (APEX2 and BioID).
source: While each of these strategies robustly label surface proteins, they: (1) require large sample inputs (biocytin hydrazide), (2) require production of genetically engineered cells (APEX2 and BioID), (3) label only partner proteins by binding targeting antibodies fused to APEX2 or horseradish peroxidase (HRP; SPPLAT), (4) require extensive sample manipulation (biocytin hydrazide), or (5) exhibit increased nonspecific labeling (NHS-ester, Table 1; Bausch-Fluck et al., 2012; Elschenbroich et al., 2010; Griffin and Schnitzer, 2011; Kuhlmann et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple sources

claim: NHS-ester labeling exhibits increased nonspecific labeling.
source: While each of these strategies robustly label surface proteins, they: (1) require large sample inputs (biocytin hydrazide), (2) require production of genetically engineered cells (APEX2 and BioID), (3) label only partner proteins by binding targeting antibodies fused to APEX2 or horseradish peroxidase (HRP; SPPLAT), (4) require extensive sample manipulation (biocytin hydrazide), or (5) exhibit increased nonspecific labeling (NHS-ester, Table 1; Bausch-Fluck et al., 2012; Elschenbroich et al., 2010; Griffin and Schnitzer, 2011; Kuhlmann et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple sources

claim: Many current surfaceomics methods are not able to capture short and transient changes that occur at the cell surface.
source: Moreover, many of these methods are not able to capture short and transient changes that occur at the cell surface, such as binding, adhesion, assembly, and signaling (Kalxdorf et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kalxdorf et al., 2017

claim: Exosomes and other small EVs are produced by both healthy and diseased cells.
source: Exosomes and other small EVs are produced by both healthy and diseased cells (Colombo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Colombo et al., 2014

claim: In cancer, small EVs contribute to tumor growth and metastasis, modulate the immune response, and mediate treatment resistance.
source: In cancer, these small EVs contribute to tumor growth and metastasis, modulate the immune response, and mediate treatment resistance (Al-Nedawi et al., 2008; Edgar, 2016; Kalluri and LeBleu, 2020; Shurtleff et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Al-Nedawi et al., 2008; Edgar, 2016; Kalluri and LeBleu, 2020; Shurtleff et al., 2018

claim: Small EVs incorporate proteins and RNA from the parent tumor from which they originate.
source: Recent studies suggest that small EVs incorporate proteins and RNA from the parent tumor from which they originate (Lin et al., 2015; Soung et al., 2017), and certain proteins may be preferentially shuttled into EVs (Poggio et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lin et al., 2015; Soung et al., 2017; Poggio et al., 2019

claim: Certain proteins may be preferentially shuttled into EVs.
source: Recent studies suggest that small EVs incorporate proteins and RNA from the parent tumor from which they originate (Lin et al., 2015; Soung et al., 2017), and certain proteins may be preferentially shuttled into EVs (Poggio et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Poggio et al., 2019

claim: Cancer-derived EVs are unique from the EVs derived from healthy surrounding tissues.
source: There is also strong evidence that cancer-derived EVs are unique from the EVs derived from healthy surrounding tissues, and therefore represent a promising target for noninvasive, early detection diagnostics, or EV-focused therapies (Kalluri and LeBleu, 2020; Skog et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kalluri and LeBleu, 2020; Skog et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2020

claim: Isolation of high-quality, enriched small EV populations is challenging, requiring numerous centrifugation steps and a final sucrose gradient isolation.
source: Isolation of high-quality, enriched small EV populations is challenging, requiring numerous centrifugation steps and a final sucrose gradient isolation, precluding the use of current labeling methods for membrane proteome characterization (Poggio et al., 2019; Shurtleff et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Poggio et al., 2019; Shurtleff et al., 2018

claim: The authors present two labeling approaches to tether exogenous peroxidases (APEX2 and HRP) directly to cells.
source: Here, we functionalize the promiscuous biotinylators, APEX2 and HRP, as noncellularly encoded exogenous membrane tethering reagents for small-scale surfaceomics, requiring <5e5 cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study

claim: The new method requires fewer than 5e5 cells.
source: Here, we functionalize the promiscuous biotinylators, APEX2 and HRP, as noncellularly encoded exogenous membrane tethering reagents for small-scale surfaceomics, requiring <5e5 cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study

claim: The new method is 10- to 100-fold more rapid than other existing protocols.
source: This method is 10- to 100-fold more rapid than other existing protocols and requires fewer wash steps with less sample loss.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study

claim: The new method requires fewer wash steps with less sample loss.
source: This method is 10- to 100-fold more rapid than other existing protocols and requires fewer wash steps with less sample loss.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study

claim: The method is not hindered by variability in individual protein glycosylation status due to its selectivity toward tyrosines.
source: Likewise, due to its selectivity toward tyrosines, it is not hindered by variability in individual protein glycosylation status (Leth-Larsen et al., 2010) or by impeding complete tryptic peptide cleavage through modification of lysines (Hacker et al., 2017), like biocytin hydrazide or NHS-biotin methods, respectively.
evidence: Supported by citations to Leth-Larsen et al., 2010 and Hacker et al., 2017

claim: The authors performed surfaceomics on cells and corresponding small EVs from a cellular model of prostate cancer using the prostate epithelial cell line, RWPE-1 with or without oncogenic Myc induction.
source: Using this robust new strategy, we performed surfaceomics on cells and corresponding small EVs from a cellular model of prostate cancer using the prostate epithelial cell line, RWPE-1 with or without oncogenic Myc induction.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study

claim: The method enabled the robust quantification of 953 cell and EV surface annotated proteins.
source: The facile WGA-HRP method permitted high surface coverage of cellular samples and enabled the first comparative surface proteome characterization of cells and cell-derived small extracellular vesicles (EVs), leading to the robust quantification of 953 cell and EV surface annotated proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study

claim: Proteins are uniquely upregulated on Myc oncogene-transformed prostate cancer EVs: ANPEP, SLC38A5, FN1, SFRP1, CDH13, THBS1, and CD44.
source: We identified a newly recognized subset of EV-enriched markers, as well as proteins that are uniquely upregulated on Myc oncogene-transformed prostate cancer EVs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study

claim: APEX2 and HRP are broadly used promiscuous proximity biotinylators that label nearby tyrosine residues in proteins through a radical intermediate mechanism using a biotin-tyramide reagent.
source: Both APEX2 and HRP are broadly used promiscuous proximity biotinylators that label nearby tyrosine residues in proteins through a radical intermediate mechanism using a biotin-tyramide reagent (Figure 1A; Hung et al., 2016; Martell et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hung et al., 2016; Martell et al., 2016 and Figure 1A

claim: HRP has been targeted to specific cell-surface proteins through antibody conjugation to label target proteins and their binding partners.
source: HRP has been targeted to specific cell-surface proteins through antibody conjugation to label target proteins and their binding partners (Rees et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rees et al., 2015

claim: HRP was used as a soluble cell surface labeler to identify rapid cell surface proteome changes in response to insulin.
source: More recently, HRP was used as a soluble cell surface labeler to identify rapid cell surface proteome changes in response to insulin (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2021

claim: Genetically encoded, membrane-targeted APEX2 and HRP have permitted promiscuous labeling of proteins in specific cellular compartments, but these efforts required cellular engineering.
source: Genetically encoded, membrane-targeted APEX2 and HRP have also permitted promiscuous labeling of proteins in specific cellular compartments, but these efforts required cellular engineering (Hung et al., 2016; Li et al., 2020a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hung et al., 2016; Li et al., 2020a

claim: The DNA-APEX2 conjugate was shown to be tethered in the presence of the lipidated DNA and not in the absence.
source: The DNA-APEX2 conjugate was shown to be tethered in the presence of the lipidated DNA (purple) and not in the absence (green), as detected by an Anti-His 680 antibody.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: WGA-HRP was incubated on Expi293 cells for 0–30 min to determine optimal incubation time on ice before labeling, and all tested times resulted in similar cell surface biotinylation efficiencies.
source: WGA-HRP was incubated on Expi293 cells for 0–30 min to determine optimal incubation time on ice before labeling. All tested times resulted in similar cell surface biotinylation efficiencies and signified that no incubation time was needed.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: 0.5 µM APEX2 produced maximal labeling of cells.
source: We found that 0.5 µM APEX2 produced maximal labeling of cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and maintained equivalent labeling across a range of cell numbers (2.5e5–1e6 cells; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: 0.5 µM APEX2 maintained equivalent labeling across a range of cell numbers (2.5e5–1e6 cells).
source: We found that 0.5 µM APEX2 produced maximal labeling of cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and maintained equivalent labeling across a range of cell numbers (2.5e5–1e6 cells; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: There was a 5- to 10-fold increase in biotin labeling for both tethered DNA-APEX2 and WGA-HRP relative to nontethered controls as assessed by flow cytometry.
source: We found a 5- to 10-fold increase in biotin labeling for both tethered DNA-APEX2 and WGA-HRP relative to nontethered controls as assessed by flow cytometry (Figure 2A) and western blotting (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2B

claim: Tethered DNA-APEX2 and WGA-HRP systems exhibited similar biotinylation efficiency.
source: Moreover, tethered DNA-APEX2 and WGA-HRP systems exhibited similar biotinylation efficiency, suggesting either system is suitable for small-scale surfaceomics.
evidence: Based on data from the study

claim: WGA-HRP identified 501 PM annotated proteins in the Uniprot Gene Ontology Cellular Component Plasma Membrane (GOCC-PM) database.
source: We observed that the WGA-HRP identified slightly more PM annotated proteins in the Uniprot Gene Ontology Cellular Component Plasma Membrane (GOCC-PM) database (>2 unique peptides, found in all replicates) relative to DNA-APEX2, totaling 501 and 467, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study

claim: DNA-APEX2 identified 467 PM annotated proteins in the Uniprot Gene Ontology Cellular Component Plasma Membrane (GOCC-PM) database.
source: We observed that the WGA-HRP identified slightly more PM annotated proteins in the Uniprot Gene Ontology Cellular Component Plasma Membrane (GOCC-PM) database (>2 unique peptides, found in all replicates) relative to DNA-APEX2, totaling 501 and 467, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study

claim: HRP identified 389 cell surface proteins.
source: Notably, the number of IDs for both cell-tethered enzymes was higher than their untethered counterparts, with HRP identifying 389 cell surface proteins and APEX2 identifying 247 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C

claim: APEX2 identified 247 cell surface proteins.
source: Notably, the number of IDs for both cell-tethered enzymes was higher than their untethered counterparts, with HRP identifying 389 cell surface proteins and APEX2 identifying 247 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The cell-tethered biotinylators showed heightened surface enrichment compared to their untethered counterparts, as illustrated by the higher overall intensities for proteins annotated to the PM.

claim: Similar normalized areas of non-glycosylated surface proteins were found across all samples (WGA-HRP, APEX2-DNA, APEX2, and HRP).

claim: The heightened labeling of WGA-HRP was consistent with every cell line tested, including another pancreatic cancer model, PaTu8902.

evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: By preincubating WGA-HRP with excess GlcNAc, the ability of WGA-HRP to label the cell surface was markedly lower than WGA-HRP without GlcNAc as observed by microscopy.

claim: Cell surface labeling in an on-plate protocol was comparable to labeling when the cells were in suspension.
source: In addition, we also tested an on-plate protocol for simpler cell surface labeling of adherent KP-4 cells. We showed that cell surface labeling in this manner was comparable to labeling when the cells were in suspension (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6

claim: Both WGA-HRP and biocytin hydrazide had similar levels of cell surface enrichment on the peptide and protein level when cross-referenced with the SURFY curated database.
source: Both WGA-HRP and biocytin hydrazide had similar levels of cell surface enrichment on the peptide and protein level when cross-referenced with the SURFY curated database for extracellular surface proteins with a predicted transmembrane domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Sulfo-NHS-LC-LC-biotin and whole-cell lysis returned the lowest percentage of cell surface enrichment.
source: Sulfo-NHS-LC-LC-biotin and whole-cell lysis returned the lowest percentage of cell surface enrichment, suggesting that a larger portion of the total sulfo-NHS-LC-LC-biotin protein identifications were of intracellular origin, despite the use of the cell-impermeable format.
evidence: Based on data from the study

claim: Biocytin hydrazide and WGA-HRP returned higher overall intensity values for SURFY-specified proteins than either sulfo-NHS-LC-LC-biotin or whole-cell lysis.

claim: The biocytin hydrazide protocol required 1.5 million cells, while WGA-HRP could be performed at 500,000 cells.

claim: All three methods (WGA-HRP, biocytin hydrazide, and sulfo-NHS-LC-LC-biotin) were highly reproducible across replicates.

claim: Prostate cancer remains one of the most common epithelial cancers in the elderly male population, especially in Western nations.

claim: Alterations in Myc occur in some of the earliest phases of prostate cancer disease, in tumor-initiating cells.
source: While metastatic progression of prostate cancer has been linked to many somatic mutations and epigenetic alterations (PTEN, p53, Myc, etc.), more recent work determined that alterations in Myc occur in some of the earliest phases of disease, that is, in tumor-initiating cells (Koh et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koh et al., 2010

claim: Small EVs are known to play important roles in the progression of prostate cancer, including increasing tumor progression, angiogenesis, metastasis, and immune evasion.

evidence: Supported by citations to Akoto and Saini, 2021; Lorenc et al., 2020; Saber et al., 2020

claim: RWPE-1 Myc cells grow with a more mesenchymal and elongated morphology compared to their Control cell counterparts.

evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Large and bidirectional variations in surfaceomes were found between Myc-induced prostate cancer and Control cells.
source: We initially used WGA-HRP to quantitatively compare the cell surface profiles of Myc-induced prostate cancer to Control cells and found large and bidirectional variations in their surfaceomes (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C and D

claim: Vimentin showed heightened expression in the context of oncogenic Myc.

evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3D and citations to Liu et al., 2015; Nakajima et al., 2004

claim: CDH2 (N-Cadherin) showed heightened expression in the context of oncogenic Myc.

evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3D and citations to Liu et al., 2015; Nakajima et al., 2004

claim: An extracellular membrane-bound form of vimentin has been found to be important in the context of cancer.

claim: ANPEP and fibronectin-1 were highly upregulated in Myc-induced cells.

claim: A number of HLA molecules were downregulated in the Myc-induced RWPE cells.

evidence: Supported by data from the study and citations to Blades et al., 1995; Cornel et al., 2020; Dhatchinamoorthy et al., 2021

claim: Myc cells produced nearly 40% more EVs than the corresponding control cells.

claim: Many of the highest intensity proteins in the EV preparation (CD9, SDCB1, CD81, LAMP1, LAMP2, ALIX, and CD63) are consistent with MVB-derived vesicle biogenesis.
source: After averaging the intensities between Control and Myc derived EVs, many of the highest intensity proteins (CD9, SDCB1, CD81, LAMP1, LAMP2, ALIX, and CD63) are consistent with MVB-derived vesicle biogenesis, supporting that the sample was likely enriched in EVs rather than other sedimentable particles that can co-isolate during centrifugation (Figure 4B).

claim: Fibronectin-1 (FN1) and ANPEP were upregulated in Myc-induced EVs.
source: This subset included fibronectin-1 (FN1) and ANPEP (Figure 4E), which were further validated by quantitative western blotting (Figure 4F).

claim: Certain proteins are shuttled to vesicle compartments largely based on the extent of expression in the parent cell (Control: IFITM3, BST2, and HLA-B, Myc: ANPEP, SLC38A5, and FN1).
source: While certain proteins are shuttled to vesicle compartments largely based on the extent of expression in the parent cell (Control: IFITM3, BST2, and HLA-B, Myc: ANPEP, SLC38A5, and FN1), remarkably some proteins are singled out for small EV packaging, indicating a pronounced differential shuttling mechanism of the proteome between cells and EVs.
evidence: Based on data from the study

claim: Some proteins are singled out for small EV packaging, indicating a pronounced differential shuttling mechanism of the proteome between cells and EVs.

claim: The majority of markers were unique to either cellular or EV origin in both the RWPE-1 Control cells and corresponding EVs, as well as the Myc cells and EVs.

claim: The WGA-HRP method allows comparison of surface proteins between small EV populations, as well as between small EV and cell samples.

claim: Secreted proteins were more highly represented in the EV surface proteome compared to cells.

claim: There are a variety of pan-prostate-EV markers, notably lactadherin (MFGE8), serotransferrin (TF), inter-alpha-trypsin inhibitor (ITIH4), immunoglobulin superfamily 8 (IGSF8), desmoglein-1 (DSG1), tetraspanin-14 (TSPAN14), and zinc-alpha-2-glycoprotein (AZGP1).

claim: Some of the pan-prostate EV targets have previously been linked to cancer-specific contexts, and this work shows they are also found on Control EVs.

claim: The fast kinetics of peroxidase enzymes (1–2 min) could enable kinetic experiments to capture rapid post-translational trafficking of surfaces proteins.
